comparator.name: Law: Business Law specialisation
comparator.sourceNotes: The September-2026 programme table and adopted TLS Appendix 1e Articles 37–45 verify the target-named Dutch-taught Law LLB specialisation and thirty compulsory components totalling sixty credits in each year. No open minor or exchange block is invented. Article 42 requires ninety degree credits for moot-court registration and at thesis teaching start. Its legacy six-credit thesis code is reconciled with the explicit eight-credit component in Article 44, the dated course entry and programme table. Non-credit Dutch testing and Talent and Career Development remain outside degree credits; the separate general-Law Skills Lab thesis rule is not imported into this specialisation.
components: The specialisation is part of the Dutch-taught Law LLB. Dutch language testing and student-development activities are non-credit requirements.
This course builds on Introduction to Business Law from Year 1 and examines the changing legal structures of companies, including investor and creditor protection, reorganisations and takeovers.
This is a compulsory 4-EC course in tax aspects of enterprise; it is not open elective space.

At least 90 degree credits must be earned at registration, not later. This pathway completes both earlier years before registration. The course develops company-law procedural documents, written legal analysis and oral pleading.

The required thesis is 8 EC, starts in autumn and spans the full academic year. Normal spring entry is not permitted. At least 90 degree credits must be earned by the start of teaching. Both earlier years are completed first. The thesis develops independent academic research on a business-law question.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target explicitly names Tilburg’s Business Law specialisation within the Law bachelor. The current official 2026–27 curriculum page confirms this exact route and supplies its complete three-year curriculum.

courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI

core: Company and business law, corporate structure, governance, shareholder relations and directors’ responsibilities
Private law, property, contracts and liability
Constitutional, criminal, administrative, European and international legal foundations
Legal practice, procedure, advocacy, research and the Business Law thesis
Corporate finance, law and economics, taxation and valuation
Organisation, strategy, business ethics and legal responsibility
European legal history and philosophy of law
adjacent: Corporate responsibility, sustainability and environmental liability
Innovative companies, entrepreneurship and legal form
questions: How should law govern mergers, shareholder disputes, directors’ liability and strategic corporate decisions?

trace: develops scholarly reading, research questions, academic writing, reflection and civic collaboration as the common foundation
develops financial statements, accounting, organisational control, accountability and discounted-cash-flow appraisal, providing actual financial analysis for enterprise decisions
examines AI, firms, regulation, corporate responsibility, labour and inequality through business and country research, providing an institutional perspective on innovative-company governance
examines legal frameworks for cross-border contracts, trade, finance, intellectual property and digital commerce, with advisory assignments and simulated arbitration

examines financial instruments, valuation, banks, risk, regulation and monetary institutions, with bank simulation and evidence-based financial decisions; it complements corporate financing rather than teaching company-law doctrine
introduces economic choice, markets, strategic interaction and government’s economic role as specific foundations for analysing regulation
examines public goods, taxation, spending, externalities and redistribution through policy models and research; this is an economic contribution rather than tax-law doctrine

examines marketing strategy, consumer psychology, responsible brands and primary/secondary evidence in business decisions; this is a complementary account of firm strategy, not legal consumer-protection training
examines trade, institutions, policy conflict and cross-border business decisions, supporting the international commercial context of legal practice
develops business models and the functions of enterprises, providing organisational context and the formal foundation for transnational business law without claiming company-law doctrine
develops empirical design, measurement, statistics and a data-collection project as a methodological complement to socio-legal inquiry
examines leadership communication, culture, persuasion and ethics through interviews, advisory work and speeches, complementing organisational responsibility and professional communication
examines motivation, leadership, teams, power, conflict and organisational change, including evidence synthesis for organisational cases
develops bargaining, interests, power, trust and strategic conflict management through negotiation simulations and scenario design
examines institutions, power, participation, justice and collective decisions in sustainability, with stakeholder consultation and policy advice/evaluation
introduces planetary boundaries and scientific methods for understanding environmental pressures and sustainability interventions
examines climate science, impacts, adaptation, mitigation, justice and governance, supplying scientific and social substance for environmental regulation
introduces legal traditions, public/private law, justice and social context through case briefs, legal interpretation, mock trials and a socio-legal proposal
examines human-rights law, protection institutions, landmark cases and philosophical justifications through legal and normative argument
examines criminal liability, punishment, criminalisation, excuses, offences and participation, with legal-advice memoranda and a criminology research proposal
examines international legal sources, state responsibility, institutions, force, human rights and treaty politics through legal cases and critical research
compares constitutional structures, rights, courts and judicial review, with administrative participation, remedies and procedural fairness
examines property, tort and contract rights across legal systems through legal briefs, comparative contract research and simulated mediation
examines EU institutions, competences, legal effect, remedies, citizenship and free movement through current judgments and legal cases
develops ethical interpretation, normative argument and independent positions on moral theory and practical questions relevant to legal judgement
examines policy-making processes and alternative analytical frameworks through a sugar-policy case and policy memos, supporting the legal-governance perspective
examines social institutions, inequality, identity and boundaries through social theory and evidence, complementing analysis of law’s social context
develops qualitative design, interviews, documentary inquiry, coding and interpretation for empirical investigation of social and institutional questions
examines environmental-justice movements, collective action and feminist/anticolonial perspectives through actual environmental cases
develops rhetorical analysis, argument construction, debating and public speaking; its communication contribution is distinguished from legal procedure
examines climate communication, public argument and contested policy through media analysis and an intervention in public debate
examines representations of ecological risk, scientific knowledge and human–environment relations as forces in public debate and environmental ethics

alternatives.distinctness: The corporate-responsibility option keeps substantial legal study and accounting, while climate, environmental governance, justice, communication and policy inquiry replace the closest option’s extended finance, marketing, international-business strategy, organisational psychology, negotiation and leadership communication. This changes sustained academic priorities rather than relabelling shared courses.

candidates.label: Corporate responsibility, sustainability and environmental liability
Innovative-company legal strategy
candidates.rationale: The innovative-company priority is already substantively covered by business foundations, AI/economic governance, finance, strategy and transnational legal study in the closest programme. No further distinct legal curriculum follows from this single priority without unrelated substitutions. No third option is added.

selection.assessment: The closest route owns the Business Law core, corporate-governance, finance, strategy and professional-practice interests. Corporate responsibility and sustainability form one evidence-backed, feasible and materially distinct second route. Innovative-company legal strategy was assessed separately, but its only generator row is already substantively implemented by the closest route and does not justify a third distinct law curriculum. Production therefore stops at two alternatives.

blocks: Legal study, business and complementary disciplines

Both develop financial analysis and investment valuation relevant to enterprise financing. UCR combines accounting and discounted-cash-flow appraisal; Tilburg applies valuation specifically to corporate-law questions.

Both develop legal-source analysis, written legal advice and oral advocacy in a simulated business dispute. UCR uses transnational arbitration; Tilburg uses company-law courtroom pleadings and Dutch procedure.

Both examine market behaviour, incentives and strategic interaction as analytical foundations. Tilburg explicitly applies economics to legal rules, transaction costs, property and corporate-law decisions.

Both examine organisations, structure, motivation and organisational decisions. UCR emphasises psychological and group dynamics; Tilburg combines organisation theory and business strategy for company-law students.
Both study methods for resolving disputes. UCR develops negotiation and bargaining through simulations; the relationship concerns dispute resolution and does not reproduce Dutch civil procedure.
Both develop legal concepts, source interpretation, case analysis and legal reasoning in social context.
Both develop substantive human-rights law and its philosophical and institutional foundations. Tilburg concentrates on the Dutch and European legal setting.
Both examine criminal acts, causation, intent, guilt, justifications, excuses and participation as grounds and limits of criminal liability.
Both provide public-international-law study. UCR applies legal sources and principles to contemporary cases and treaty politics; this is a partial subject relationship.
Both examine state organisation, rights and constitutional constraints. UCR uses comparison and includes administrative principles; Tilburg establishes Dutch constitutional foundations.
Both develop property, contract and tort concepts through legal cases. UCR compares legal systems while Tilburg establishes the Dutch private-law foundations.
Both examine the EU legal order, national effects, citizenship, free movement and remedies. Tilburg additionally addresses competition law and procurement.
Both develop normative analysis of responsibility and competing obligations. UCR provides ethical theory and argument; Tilburg applies ethics specifically to enterprise.
No selected course centres European legal history.
No additional selected course provides this dedicated Dutch-law component; broader legal study is placed with its strongest substantive counterpart elsewhere.

No selected UCR course supplies Tilburg’s sustained Dutch company-law sequence in legal structures, shareholder/creditor protection, reorganisations and takeovers. Transnational Business Law has its strongest direct relationship with simulated legal-dispute practice.
No additional selected course provides this dedicated Dutch-law component; broader legal study is placed with its strongest substantive counterpart elsewhere.
General ethics has its strongest relationship with enterprise ethics. No additional course provides the specific legal-philosophical component.
No additional selected course provides this dedicated Dutch-law component; broader legal study is placed with its strongest substantive counterpart elsewhere.
Economic analysis of taxation is not the dedicated legal treatment of enterprise taxation.

Organisational and economic perspectives on work do not substitute for Dutch individual and collective labour-law doctrine.
The eight-credit business-law thesis is compulsory. Optional UCR independent research is displayed separately outside scheduled credits.

notes.text: UCR can combine substantial comparative and international law with business, finance, ethics and environmental governance. Tilburg provides a dedicated Dutch company-law, tax and procedural sequence and a compulsory legal thesis. The partial relationships shown do not reproduce that specialist training or confer legal professional qualification.

audience.programmeDescription: Tilburg’s Business Law specialisation combines the broad Law LLB with sustained company-law study, finance, economics, organisation and ethics. The Dutch-taught programme requires legal practice and an eight-credit business-law thesis; its standard curriculum has no unallocated elective block.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR can connect substantial legal study with financial and organisational analysis or with corporate responsibility and sustainability. Its law courses mainly use comparative and international approaches. Tilburg provides deeper Dutch company-law and procedural training; the relationships shown are partial and do not replace its required thesis.
